policies.summary: Privately developed wind and solar facilities are exempt from Power Review Board approval once the owner files certifications (including local decommissioning compliance and, above 10 MW, a public meeting), leaving siting to county and city zoning; the board must still approve generation built by public power suppliers and private energy storage.

restrictions.description: Butler County has no zoning; a countywide survey (~800 responses) found roughly 90% support for a moratorium on the top land uses of concern (wind, solar, data centers, battery storage, landfill), following years of unregulated development including the in-progress Sandhills Energy solar project. Active as of 2026-09-23, though modified: adopted 2026-03-16 as a 9-month moratorium (through approximately 2026-12-15) on wind, solar, data center, battery storage, and landfill land uses while the county completes a comprehensive plan and zoning regulations (targeted for completion around September 2026). Per Flatwater Free Press, after the threat of a lawsuit the county later exempted the ongoing Sandhills Energy solar project (which had been under development since 2019) from the moratorium. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-07 (Butler County Board of Supervisors), mirroring the Planning Commission's Resolution 2026-04 but striking language that would have excluded projects already under construction.

restrictions.description: Resident concerns raised at public comment about health, safety, and property-value impacts of proposed solar energy farms. Active as of 2026-09-23. Resolution No. 2026-08, adopted 2026-06-23 on a 6-1 vote, imposes a 6-month moratorium on accepting new conditional-use-permit applications for solar energy farms (through approximately 2026-12-23) and directs the Planning Commission to review the comprehensive plan/zoning regulations (setbacks, infrasound, health concerns, property-value impacts, 'occupied dwelling' definition, etc.) and report recommendations within 4 months. Existing operations and already-issued pending permits are not affected. Legal basis: Resolution No. 2026-08 (Fillmore County Board of Supervisors).

restrictions.description: County zoning regulations not sufficient to address commercial wind/solar projects. Adopted 2025-08-26; a temporary moratorium on wind energy installations and solar power generation systems. No data-center-specific moratorium was located for Furnas County despite Nebraska Public Media listing the county among those with data center moratoria in place. [VERIFY details not confirmed at confidence 0.55 in the 2026-09 refresh]. Legal basis: Resolution 2025-8-26.

Regulatory-gap/preemptive: county attorney and chair described ongoing work to update the county's comprehensive plan and zoning regulations (targeted for completion by May 2027) and encouraged public participation in town-hall meetings on the update; the proposed moratorium would pause applications while that update is completed. Pending as of 2026-09-23. The Sept. 8, 2026 board agenda listed 'Consider imposing a 12 month moratorium on the acceptance of applications for wind energy systems, solar energy systems, battery energy storage systems, cryptocurrency-mining operations, data centers, artificial intelligence facilities, carbon dioxide capture, transport, and sequestration facilities, high-voltage transmission infrastructure, and other utility scale or specialized technology facilities superseding Resolution 2025-8.' At the Sept. 8 meeting the board discussed the item but did not vote (no resolution number was assigned in the minutes for this item, unlike the numbered resolutions that followed for other business). At the Sept. 21, 2026 meeting, the item returned as 'proposed Resolution 26-18'; the minutes record discussion but 'No action taken at this time.' No adoption vote had occurred as of the last confirmed meeting (Sept. 21, 2026), two days before this research date. [VERIFY adoption date not confirmed at confidence 0.6 in the 2026-09 refresh]. Legal basis: Proposed Resolution 26-18 (not yet adopted as of 2026-09-21), described in the Sept. 8, 2026 agenda as superseding 'Resolution 2025-8'.

restrictions.description: regulatory_gap: broad pause covering utility-scale and specialized technology facilities pending county zoning/regulatory development. Active as of 2026-09-23. Resolution 2026-11, adopted 2026-06-10, imposes a 12-month moratorium on acceptance of applications for wind and solar energy systems, battery energy storage systems, cryptocurrency-mining operations, data centers, artificial intelligence facilities, carbon dioxide capture/transport/sequestration facilities, and high-voltage electric transmission infrastructure; it supersedes the county's prior 2025 moratorium resolutions (2025-19, 2025-21, 2025-25). Legal basis: Resolution 2026-11 (McPherson County Board of Commissioners), superseding Resolutions 2025-19, 2025-21, and 2025-25.

restrictions.description: regulatory_gap: the county's zoning regulations do not yet address commercial-scale renewable energy systems; the moratorium is intended to remain in place only until new zoning regulations governing such systems are formally adopted and become legally binding. Active as of 2026-09-23. This is a distinct, longer-running moratorium from the county's separate 2026-06-30 data-center-specific moratorium already in the inventory (ne-seward-county-2026, Resolution 3937): this row covers commercial wind, solar, and battery-generated energy projects, was first imposed 2023-08-01, and has been repeatedly extended by the Board (including at its Jan. 6, 2026 meeting). Most recently, the Board voted 2026-08-25 (Resolution No. 3947, unanimous) to continue the moratorium for six more months from that date (to approximately 2027-02-25) or until new zoning regulations are adopted and legally binding, whichever comes first. It applies to solar systems of 500kW AC or greater and wind systems serving off-site customers/community/grid. Legal basis: Resolution No. 3947 (Seward County Board of Commissioners, adopted 2026-08-25), continuing the moratorium first imposed 2023-08-01 and repeatedly renewed since (cites Neb. Rev. Stat. section 23-114).

restrictions.long_description: As of May 2020, the Brown County Zoning Regulations require that commercial wind turbines be set back 1 mile from property lines and roads.

restrictions.description: In March 2023, the Buffalo County Commissioners adopted new setback requirements for wind turbines that require distances of: 2 miles from any burial site or the Platte River; 3 miles from any agriculture residential zoned property; 3 miles from property lines of nonparticipants; 3 miles from any church, hospital, pool, or park; 5 miles from any village or city; 5 miles from any wildlife preservation area.
restrictions.long_description: In March 2023, the Buffalo County Commissioners adopted new setback requirements for wind turbines that require distances of: 2 miles from any burial site or the Platte River; 3 miles from any agriculture residential zoned property; 3 miles from property lines of nonparticipants; 3 miles from any church, hospital, pool, or park; 5 miles from any village or city; 5 miles from any wildlife preservation area.

restrictions.description: In December 2024, the Burt County Board of Supervisors adopted new zoning regulations that require commercial wind turbines to be set back 3 miles from any towns or villages, 1 mile from property lines, and 0.5 miles from any occupied dwelling.
restrictions.long_description: In December 2024, the Burt County Board of Supervisors adopted new zoning regulations that require commercial wind turbines to be set back 3 miles from any towns or villages, 1 mile from property lines, and 0.5 miles from any occupied dwelling. The ordinance further limits the number of turbines in the county to a cumulative total of 20 turbines, prohibits shadow flicker on roads, and provides that noise shall not exceed 40 dBA from any dwelling on a nonparticipating property, except during periods of severe weather.

restrictions.long_description: Cedar County’s zoning ordinance, last updated in June 2022, requires commercial wind turbines to be set back at least one mile from non-participating dwelling units, public conservation lands, and other existing commercial wind turbines not owned by the applicant.

restrictions.description: On July 26, 2021, Dakota County amended its zoning regulations to require that commercial wind turbines be set back 2 miles from neighboring dwelling units (up from 2,700 feet) and 2 miles from wetlands and other conservation lands (up from 600 feet).
restrictions.long_description: On July 26, 2021, Dakota County amended its zoning regulations to require that commercial wind turbines be set back 2 miles from neighboring dwelling units (up from 2,700 feet) and 2 miles from wetlands and other conservation lands (up from 600 feet).

restrictions.description: In November 2022, Dawson County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind farm applications.
restrictions.long_description: In November 2022, Dawson County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind farm applications. In May 2023, the Dawson County Board of Commissioners adopted amendments to its wind regulations that impose setbacks of 3 miles from non-participating property lines, participating dwellings, road rights-of-way, and public conservation lands. The regulations also limit noise to 40 dBa at the nearest dwelling.

restrictions.description: In September 2015, Franklin Township implemented regulations requiring that wind turbines be set back 1,640 feet from public roads and non-participating private property lines.
restrictions.long_description: In September 2015, Franklin Township implemented regulations requiring that wind turbines be set back 1,640 feet from public roads and non-participating private property lines. The regulations were drafted by a group called Bohemian Alps Wind Watchers and implemented around the same time by five other townships in Butler County. On October 5, 2015, Butler County sent a letter to the townships challenging their authority to implement such regulations and requesting that they void the regulations. Several townships responded by stating that they would not void the regulations, but Franklin was not among them.

restrictions.description: Gage County adopted a moratorium on new permits for wind farms and banned commercial wind turbines within 1 mile of property lines.
restrictions.long_description: In July 2020, Gage County adopted a 3-month moratorium on new permits for wind farms. In November 2021, Gage County adopted amendments that banned commercial wind turbines within 1 mile of property lines of non-participating property owners, a major change from the 2019 zoning regulations, which required only that turbines be set back from property lines by a distance of 2 times turbine height. Gage County subsequently imposed an indefinite moratorium on commercial solar facilities in 2022 to halt solar development while considering new solar restrictions.

restrictions.description: In April 2024, the Greeley County Board of Commissioners adopted a 3-year moratorium on renewable energy applications.
restrictions.long_description: In April 2024, the Greeley County Board of Commissioners adopted a 3-year moratorium on renewable energy applications.

restrictions.description: Hamilton County ordinance requires that wind turbines be set back 2 miles from property lines of non-participating landowners.
restrictions.long_description: Hamilton County ordinance requires that wind turbines be set back 2 miles from property lines of non-participating landowners.

restrictions.description: Holt County amended its zoning ordinance in November 2022 to require commercial wind turbines to be set back at least 1 mile from neighboring dwelling units.
restrictions.long_description: Holt County amended its zoning ordinance in November 2022 to require commercial wind turbines to be set back at least 1 mile from neighboring dwelling units.

restrictions.description: An ordinance last amended in January 2016 provides that solar farms of 25 kW or larger must be set back at least 1,320 feet from neighboring dwelling units.
restrictions.long_description: An ordinance last amended in January 2016 provides that solar farms of 25 kW or larger must be set back at least 1,320 feet from neighboring dwelling units.

restrictions.description: In 2015, Lancaster County adopted updates to its zoning code to require that wind turbines maintain noise limits of 40 dBa in the day and 37 dBa at night at non-participating dwellings.
restrictions.long_description: In 2015, Lancaster County adopted updates to its zoning code to require that wind turbines maintain noise limits of 40 dBa in the day and 37 dBa at night at non-participating dwellings. The county also set the following setback requirements: 2 times turbine height from non-participating property lines, 3.5 times turbine height from non-participating dwellings, and 2 times turbine height from participating dwellings. The county defined turbine height as hub height plus rotor radius. In 2019, Lancaster County once again updated its wind energy regulations to require a 1-mile setback from non-participating dwellings.

restrictions.description: On October 28, 2020, the Wheeler County Commissioners voted to prohibit “Commercial/Utility Grade Wind Energy Systems.” On November 25, 2020, the county attorney informed the commissioners that their vote to completely prohibit utility-scale wind was unconstitutional and advised them to consider other restrictions.
restrictions.long_description: On October 28, 2020, the Wheeler County Commissioners voted to prohibit “Commercial/Utility Grade Wind Energy Systems.” On November 25, 2020, the county attorney informed the commissioners that their vote to completely prohibit utility-scale wind was unconstitutional and advised them to consider other restrictions. On December 9, 2020, the commissioners voted to require a 5-mile setback from any dwelling, to cap turbine height at 299 feet, and to require a distance of 0.5 miles between turbines.

restrictions.description: Since October 2019 or earlier, Thomas County has required that wind turbines be set back 3 miles from property lines, roads, and wetlands, and limited noise to 35 dbA at the nearest occupied structure.
restrictions.long_description: Since October 2019 or earlier, Thomas County has required that wind turbines be set back 3 miles from property lines, roads, and wetlands, and limited noise to 35 dbA at the nearest occupied structure.

Stanton County: Setback Restriction (wind)

In November 2017, the county effectively banned new wind farms by approving a land use matrix that does not allow developers to obtain any type of permit for commercial wind energy systems in any zone.
restrictions.long_description: In November 2017, the county effectively banned new wind farms by approving a land use matrix that does not allow developers to obtain any type of permit for commercial wind energy systems in any zone. The ordinance also requires setbacks of 2,700 feet from nonparticipating residences, but the requirement appears to be moot in light of the complete exclusion of new wind farms.

restrictions.description: The Saline County Zoning Regulations, as amended in 2018, require that wind turbines be set back 0.5 miles from occupied structures on abutting properties.
restrictions.long_description: The Saline County Zoning Regulations, as amended in 2018, require that wind turbines be set back 0.5 miles from occupied structures on abutting properties. The regulations further limit noise to 40 dBA for any 10-minute average at any dwelling. In August 2020, the Saline County Planning and Zoning Board approved a 4-month moratorium on new wind farm applications. After the 6-1 vote, the Board stated that the moratorium was meant to ensure community safety and the sustainable future development of wind energy in Saline County.

restrictions.description: In January 2023, Red Willow County enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar farms with the option to extend.
restrictions.long_description: In January 2023, Red Willow County enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar farms with the option to extend. The moratorium was enacted amidst local concerns about a proposed 54-MW solar plant north of McCook.

restrictions.long_description: In November 2017, Pierce County commissioners extended a moratorium on wind farm applications that had been put in place in June 2017 to June 2018.

restrictions.long_description: Otoe County’s zoning ordinance requires commercial wind turbines to be set back at least 1 mile from non-participating property lines, churches, and schools, and at least 2 miles from village and city limits. On January 31, 2023, the Otoe County Commissioners adopted new restrictions on wind energy: according to the meeting minutes, “turbines shall be limited to no more than two WECS per participating landowner within a one (1) mile radius of the participating property line.”

restrictions.description: In April 2024, the Otoe County Board of Commissioners enacted a moratorium on conditional use permits for commercial solar projects, which was extended in May 2024 and August 2024.
restrictions.long_description: In April 2024, the Otoe County Board of Commissioners enacted a moratorium on conditional use permits for commercial solar projects, which was extended in May 2024 and August 2024. In December 2024, Otoe County voted to approve zoning regulations that allow commercial solar on up to 1% of the county’s total acres. The regulations also require a 1,000-foot setback from non-participating dwellings. Several citizens speaking at the public hearing stated that they opposed seeing solar panels on land once used for agricultural purposes.

In March 2023, Lincoln County established a 1-year moratorium in order to consider how to regulate utility-scale wind and solar.
restrictions.long_description: In March 2023, Lincoln County established a 1-year moratorium in order to consider how to regulate utility-scale wind and solar. The County Commissioners delayed a vote on new regulations in October 2023 amidst intense opposition at a local hearing, agreeing instead to extend the moratorium for 1.5 years

restrictions.description: In May 2024, the Knox County Board of Supervisors voted 5-1 to change setback rules for wind turbines from 2,000 feet to 6,600 feet from nonparticipating dwellings.
restrictions.long_description: In May 2024, the Knox County Board of Supervisors voted 5-1 to change setback rules for wind turbines from 2,000 feet to 6,600 feet from nonparticipating dwellings. A wind energy company, which had been working to develop a 600-MW project in the county, filed a lawsuit against the county alleging that the zoning rule changes were made “with the express purpose of regulating” the wind energy company and its proposed wind project. On May 7, 2025, the Planning Commission voted to recommend a ban on commercial wind and solar development in the county. On June 11, 2025, the County Board of Supervisors voted to adopt the Planning Commission’s recommendation to ban any new commercial wind or solar projects. See entry on North Fork Wind (Knox County) for more information.

restrictions.description: In April 2022, Jefferson County established a moratorium on permits for wind energy projects as it considered updates to its wind regulations.
restrictions.long_description: In April 2022, Jefferson County established a moratorium on permits for wind energy projects as it considered updates to its wind regulations. On March 23, 2023, Jefferson County adopted a new wind ordinance that requires turbines to be set back 1 mile from incorporated towns, schools, churches, state owned recreation areas, and the homes of any nonparticipating landowners.

restrictions.description: In September 2015, Savannah Township implemented regulations requiring that wind turbines be set back 1,640 feet from public roads and non-participating private property lines.
restrictions.long_description: In September 2015, Savannah Township implemented regulations requiring that wind turbines be set back 1,640 feet from public roads and non-participating private property lines. The regulations were drafted by a group called Bohemian Alps Wind Watchers and implemented around the same time by five other townships in Butler County. On October 5, 2015, Butler County sent a letter to the townships challenging their authority to implement such regulations and requesting that they void the regulations. Several townships responded by stating that they would not void the regulations, but Savannah was not among them.

projects.description: New York-based Con Edison’s plans to build an 86-turbine wind farm in Burt County encountered opposition from individuals who organized against the project on a Facebook group called “Burt County, NE Citizens United.” Sometime around 2020, the county adopted the restrictive setbacks described above.
projects.long_description: New York-based Con Edison’s plans to build an 86-turbine wind farm in Burt County encountered opposition from individuals who organized against the project on a Facebook group called “Burt County, NE Citizens United.” Sometime around 2020, the county adopted the restrictive setbacks described above. There is no news coverage about the project from after 2020, but a tracker on a Nebraska government website states that the facility may come to the county as soon as 2023.

projects.description: NextEra Energy Resources is developing the 41-turbine, 115-MW Greeley Wind project.
projects.long_description: NextEra Energy Resources is developing the 41-turbine, 115-MW Greeley Wind project. NextEra has planned for the project to begin operations by December 2026, subject to local and state approvals. The Greeley County Board of Commissioners approved a special use permit for NextEra despite the vocal opposition. Opponents voiced health concerns related to noise, vibrations, and shadow flicker generated by the turbines; environmental concerns related to the concrete bases and decommissioning of blades; and economic concerns related to property values and farm income. Local residents voiced opposition on the Facebook group Greeley County Alliance for Wise Energy.

projects.description: OPPD energy has proposed a 310-MW solar project in York County called K-Junction Solar.
projects.long_description: OPPD energy has proposed a 310-MW solar project in York County called K-Junction Solar. In October 2023, over 100 residents attended a meeting at which many residents expressed concern about the project’s environmental and economic impacts, including impacts on the local agriculture industry, while other residents supported the potential for agrivoltaics and potential positive impacts on the local economy. A Facebook group called “STOP K-Junction Solar” formed in opposition to the project, and in November 2023, a Nebraska resident submitted an op-ed opposing the project to the York News Times.

projects.description: In July 2016, the Cherry County Planning Commission formally recommended against granting a conditional land use permit to Bluestem Sandhills to construct the Kilgore Wind Project, which was then planned to be a 30-turbine wind farm in Cherry County.
projects.long_description: In July 2016, the Cherry County Planning Commission formally recommended against granting a conditional land use permit to Bluestem Sandhills to construct the Kilgore Wind Project, which was then planned to be a 30-turbine wind farm in Cherry County. The decision was made at a meeting attended by over 200 individuals that lasted until 2:00 a.m. A local opposition group raised arguments about potential impacts on birds and wetlands. In October 2019, the Cherry County Board granted a conditional use permit to a 19-turbine plan for the project. A group called Preserve the Sandhills LLC, which claimed to have 500 members, filed an appeal challenging the decision in Cherry County District Court the following month. In August 2020, District Judge Kosizek denied a motion to dismiss, allowing the suit to proceed. In June 2020, the Cherry County Board granted a 4-year extension for the completion of the wind turbine project while the suit was pending, which the project opponents claimed was improper. However, the Cherry County District Court held that it did not have jurisdiction to consider objections to the extension, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court of Nebraska in 2021. On February 24, 2023, the Nebraska Supreme Court dismissed appeals from Preserve the Sandhills LLC, paving the way for the project to move forward.

projects.description: In November 2019, a group of Saline County residents sued to block this 99-turbine, 300-MW wind farm, arguing that a conditional use permit issued to the original owner could not be transferred to the new owner.
projects.long_description: In November 2019, a group of Saline County residents sued to block this 99-turbine, 300-MW wind farm, arguing that a conditional use permit issued to the original owner could not be transferred to the new owner. The lawsuit failed to stop the project, which became operational in 2021. In July 2021, The Board of Adjustments, in response to an appeal by a landowner, ordered that wind turbines may not operate above 50 dBa within 1000 feet of the landowner’s property or be subject to a shut down. In a challenge brought by Milligan, a Saline County District Judge granted a temporary injunction until the merits of the case are determined. The litigation is still ongoing.

projects.description: In early 2024, a group of people referring to themselves as the “Wind Watchers” organized opposition to a proposed 600-MW commercial wind energy project in Knox County, which had been under development since 2017.
projects.long_description: In early 2024, a group of people referring to themselves as the “Wind Watchers” organized opposition to a proposed 600-MW commercial wind energy project in Knox County, which had been under development since 2017. In May 2024, the Knox County Board of Supervisors voted to increase the setback requirements for wind from 2,000 feet to 6,600 feet from nonparticipating dwellings. North Fork Wind responded by filing a lawsuit in federal court, which alleged, among other claims, that the zoning amendments violated the contracts clause, the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment and Nebraska Constitution, the due process clause of the 14th Amendment, and the takings clause of the Fifth Amendment and Nebraska Constitution. [Note: In March 2025, the court dismissed all of the claims except the takings claim.]

projects.description: In May 2021, the Saunders County Board voted to approve a permit for an 81-MW, 500-acre solar project by Community Energy.
projects.long_description: In May 2021, the Saunders County Board voted to approve a permit for an 81-MW, 500-acre solar project by Community Energy. Opponents collected 500 signatures against the project, and 45 landowners retained an attorney to consider legal action.

projects.description: Ranger Power’s plans to construct a 250-MW solar project on 2,800 acres east of Lincoln encountered opposition from neighbors.
projects.long_description: Ranger Power’s plans to construct a 250-MW solar project on 2,800 acres east of Lincoln encountered opposition from neighbors. One county commissioner proposed an amendment to prohibit solar panels on a portion of the project within city limits, but the amendment was defeated. In January 2022, a local newspaper reported that four landowners had filed notices of appeal in Lancaster County District Court challenging the Lancaster County Board’s approval of the project. In November 2022, nearly three dozen landowners filed a lawsuit challenging the county’s approval of the project.

projects.description: In 2021, NextEra Energy proposed to develop the 1.5-MW Cass County solar project on approximately 2,000 acres of farmland west of Murray.
projects.long_description: In 2021, NextEra Energy proposed to develop the 1.5-MW Cass County solar project on approximately 2,000 acres of farmland west of Murray. In February 2025, the Cass County Board denied a conditional use permit for the project, citing local opposition to it based on concerns about its impact on property values. The Board also noted that the priority of the county’s development plan is to preserve agriculture.

projects.description: In 2024, NextEra Energy proposed the 304-MW Panama Energy Center to be developed on 2,400 acres of land in Lincoln, Lancaster County.
projects.long_description: In 2024, NextEra Energy proposed the 304-MW Panama Energy Center to be developed on 2,400 acres of land in Lincoln, Lancaster County. Local residents raised concerns over the project’s impact on the character of the neighborhood and the loss of agricultural land. In January 2025, the project was approved by the Lincoln Planning Commission. In December 2025, project opponents filed a lawsuit in the Nebraska District Court challenging the approval of the project. The district court ruled that the Commission had properly approved the project as it was compatible with the existing permitted land uses. In March 2026, the project opponents appealed the district court ruling to the Nebraska Court of Appeals. The appeal remains pending as of June 2026.
